data.title: P. Šalkovský: Chieftains, princes and kings of the Slavs of Slovakia and Moravia and their seats of power
data.excerpt: From the Slavic migrations of the 5th century to the fall of Great Moravia, Peter Šalkovský traces how the leaders of the Slavs of Slovakia and Moravia rose from tribal chieftains elected by an assembly to princes and kings. He also shows where they resided: at first in ordinary open settlements, later in the strongholds of Mikulčice, Staré Město and Nitra, with their palace buildings, churches and magnates’ manorial courts.
data.metaTitle: Šalkovský: Slavic princes and their strongholds
data.metaDescription: Peter Šalkovský on the chieftains, princes and kings of the Slavs of Slovakia and Moravia and on their strongholds, from the Slavic expansion to Great Moravia.

keyFacts.label: Author
keyFacts.value: PhDr. Peter Šalkovský, DrSc., Institute of Archaeology of the Slovak Academy of Sciences in Nitra

keyFacts.label: Period
keyFacts.value: 5th–10th century (from the Slavic migrations to the fall of Great Moravia)

keyFacts.label: First prince attested in writing
keyFacts.value: Pribina (c. 800–861), prince of the Principality of Nitra

timeline.title: Samo becomes leader of the tribal confederation
timeline.description: The Frankish merchant Samo became the leader of a tribal confederation later called Samo’s Empire by historiography.

timeline.title: The battle at Wogastisburg
timeline.description: The oldest written record, in the Chronicle of Fredegar, notes a military encounter with the Franks at a fortified place called Wogastisburg, in the territory of Samo’s Empire.

timeline.title: Samo’s death and the collapse of his empire
timeline.description: After Samo’s death his supra-tribal polity disintegrated; although Samo is said to have had 22 sons, none of them managed to gain the necessary authority among the tribes.

timeline.title: Pribina as prince of the Principality of Nitra
timeline.description: Pribina was prince of the independent Principality of Nitra, with its seat at Nitra (Nitrava).

timeline.title: Mojmír I annexes the Principality of Nitra
timeline.description: Mojmír I forced Pribina to flee from Nitra and, by annexing the Principality of Nitra, became ruler of Great Moravia; the polity later called Great Moravia came into being.

timeline.title: Pribina receives the Pannonian principality
timeline.description: Pribina received from the East Frankish ruler Louis the German, in administration and later in lifelong tenure, the territory called the Pannonian principality, where he launched colonisation and Christianisation.

timeline.title: Louis the German deposes Mojmír I
timeline.description: Louis the German deposed Mojmír I and installed his nephew Rastislav in his place.

timeline.title: The arrival of Constantine and Methodius
timeline.description: Rastislav and Svatopluk summoned the Byzantine scholars Constantine and Methodius to Great Moravia; Constantine created the Glagolitic script for the needs of the Slavic language.

timeline.title: The end of the reign of Prince Rastislav
timeline.description: Rastislav’s reign, which had lasted since 846, came to an end.

timeline.title: The death of Prince Koceľ
timeline.description: Koceľ, the son of Pribina and his successor in the Pannonian principality, died.

timeline.title: The first bishopric in the territory of Slovakia
timeline.description: At the latest from 880, Nitra was the seat of the first bishopric in the territory of Slovakia, headed by Wiching.

timeline.title: The death of King Svatopluk
timeline.description: The reign of Svatopluk, who became ruler of Great Moravia after Rastislav, ended with his death.

children.text: The migrations of the Slavic tribes to the west, the taking of new homelands – also called the Slavic “expansion” – were the movements, in stages, of individual tribes and parts of them into new territories, their occupation and colonisation. They lasted from the second half of the 5th century throughout the whole of the 6th century, and in some zones continued into the 7th–8th centuries. The resettlement proceeded in several waves, in various directions and with varying intensity. Very probably these resettlements, reaching dimensions of several hundred kilometres, were carried out under the leadership of tribal chieftains or of individuals enjoying majority authority, just as was the case with the Germanic tribes or their detached segments in the first half of the 1st millennium. Even though this certainly cannot be compared in full, because, unlike the predominantly farming Slavic communities, the Germanic peoples had a considerably more militarised structure of society. The movements of larger groups of population certainly required a certain “logistical” preparation – the gathering of the most essential materials, movable property, tools and food supplies, the choice of the destination and the season of the move, the route and the organisation of the journey, including the overcoming of natural obstacles, whether rivers, wetlands, forests or mountain ranges.

The main currents of the Slavic migration were directed to the south-west, towards the lower Danube and the peripheral provinces of Byzantium. From the second half of the 6th century, written sources give us some of the names of their tribal chieftains, dukes or rulers (rex Daurentius – Dauritas /Dobreta?/; Medzamir, son of Idaridzios and brother of Kelagast; the leaders Pirogastos and Ardagast; rega – rex Musocius /Mužok?/). Several communities from the core of the Slavic homeland, in the territories of present-day Ukraine and Belarus, began at some point in the second half of the 5th century to move westwards as well, and settled first of all the basin of the upper Vistula. Soon afterwards, after 470 – following the destruction of the Suebian kingdom in the north-western part of the Carpathian Basin by the Ostrogoths – some of them departed through the passes of the Western Carpathians into Slovakia, or moved further west across the Polish lowlands. The influx of settlement certainly continued more intensively in the first half of the 6th century.

The first groups of Slavs reached the middle Morava region in the second half of the 6th century, coming from the middle Váh region across the White Carpathians. The territories north of the middle Danube – especially Slovakia and Moravia – were therefore not only settled by related groups of early Slavic population with the Prague culture, but in the following centuries (7th–8th) also had a similar development, in close neighbourhood to and under the strong influence of the Avar Khaganate. A stratum of local chieftainly elites can be assumed here with certainty at the latest in connection with the rise of Samo’s Empire, its conflicts with the Frankish Empire and the Avar Khaganate. This is also indicated by the oldest written record, in the Chronicle of Fredegar, of a military encounter with the Franks at some point in 631/632 in the territory of Samo’s Empire, at a fortified place called Wogastisburg. The creation of such fortifications – even though these may have been only temporary timber-and-earth defences built “ad hoc” for short-term defensive use, as assembly places for armies in time of war – already required a certain higher form of social organisation allowing the concentration of manpower and materials (timber, earth, stones) for their construction. And therefore also at least their temporary administrators and commanders. In times of peace they were probably abandoned, or served only to protect merchant caravans or as cult places, but not yet as permanently occupied centres of tribes and seats of tribal nobilities. These probably resided in open settlements. The first and only leader mentioned by name, under whose administration south-western Slovakia and southern Moravia evidently belonged, was Samo (* c. 600 – † 658/659), a merchant from the Frankish Empire. In 623 Samo became the leader of a tribal confederation designated by historiography as Samo’s Empire. He arrived in the company of other Frankish merchants. Merchant expeditions of that time must have been composed of militarily capable individuals, or accompanied by an armed retinue, because they not infrequently became the target of robbery by the inhabitants of the regions through which they passed.

children.text: The Slavs north of the Danube, their representatives, the local tribal chieftains and other representatives of the kindreds – that is, the tribal assembly – elected him as their leader (the title rex – king is recorded) in 623, after he had distinguished himself in the fighting during the Slavic uprising against the Avars. Unfortunately we do not know the names of these, nor of any other local chieftains in Moravia and Slovakia, who were elected by the tribal assembly with the assistance, or even under the patronage, of pagan priests.

There are no reliable historical sources on Samo’s later life. After his death in 658 or 659 his supra-tribal polity disintegrated. Although Samo is said to have had 22 sons, probably not one of them was capable of continuing his rule, or rather none managed to gain the necessary authority among the tribes.

For the 6th–7th centuries we so far know of larger ground-level buildings that might be regarded as the dwellings and seats of Slavic leaders only exceptionally, from the lower Danube region. It may be assumed that, especially in the troubled times of migrations and military campaigns and in the close neighbourhood of the Avars, the conditions for building more solid, permanent and representative seats of tribal chieftains of the “palace” type were still only rarely created; one may rather think of more or less provisional, lightweight structures serving as assembly and council spaces for the prince – the chieftain – his suite and the representatives of the tribe.

The present state of research allows the assumption that both free warriors who had acquired a certain higher social status and other more influential individuals without chieftainly powers, who were temporarily authorised by the community in times of crisis or war, could have resided within ordinary unfortified settlements. Their dwellings might be indicated by certain phenomena, or rather by the co-occurrence of these, observed on settlement sites. These are markedly larger ground-plan dimensions of the dwelling, the furnishing of the house, the central position of the house within the settlement, an evident link of several ancillary features to the house, as well as the presence of objects of a “luxury” character. Such an interpretation is also supported by the rarity of larger sunken-featured buildings – dwellings with their floor sunk into a pit – among the Slavs in general: only about 5% of the known ground plans are sunken-featured buildings with a living area of over 20 m². In the 8th century, too, such houses are rare in the territory of present-day Slovakia and are probably linked to the more advanced Slavic–Avar milieu.

Evidence for the existence of local elites in the territory of present-day Slovakia and Moravia, at the latest during the course of the 8th century, we have north of the Avar territory, in the regions of the later core of Great Moravia, in the form of the first strongholds. Today these are mostly called hradisko, horodišče, grodzisko, gorodišče or Burgwall, to distinguish them from the later masonry castles of the High Middle Ages. Their original name throughout the whole period of their existence was, however, in the Slavic languages gord, grad, grod, gorod, and in German Purch, Burg – as for example Veligrad, Königsburg, civitas Kesigesburch, Starigard/Oldenburg, Jaromarsburg, Wogastisburg, Mosapurc/Blatengrad, Lautenpurch, Lundenburg and the like, or also in the names of early Hungarian centres of Slavic origin such as Vissegrad, Nógrád, Crngrad. For understandable reasons, however, without the names of their leaders. There was no one to record them: the Slavs of the Middle Danube region did not yet have writing, nor did they yet interest Frankish politicians and their chroniclers.

children.text: In this period a “stronghold” of simple timber-and-earth construction with a palisade arose at Uherské Hradiště and also at Olomouc. In the second half, or at the end, of the 8th century strongholds evidently already existed at Mikulčice, Brno-Líšeň and perhaps some others as well. Several finds from Svätý Jur suggest that Slavic strongholds could have arisen very early even within the territory of the Avar Khaganate.

When the Avar Khaganate collapsed at the turn of the 8th and 9th centuries, destroyed by Frankish armies and their Slavic allies, a favourable situation arose throughout the Carpathian Basin, including the Drava–Sava region and the northern Balkans, for the concentration of power and surplus product in the hands of local Slavic princes, for the emergence of military retinues and for their more marked social separation from the milieu of the village communities. The simultaneous shift of the borders of the Frankish Empire as far as Pannonia, or rather the Middle Danube region, meant the entry of the territory of present-day Slovakia and Moravia not only into the sphere of this great power’s immediate political interest, but also into its secular and ecclesiastical organisation. This must have had a considerable influence on all spheres of life, above all on the social elites as the main receptor and bearer of economic, social and cultural change. The outward, or archaeologically traceable, manifestations of these changes included the adoption of the Christian burial rite and the building of the first churches and of fortified seats on Frankish models.

This is also confirmed by written reports of the existence of several princes (principes Sclavorum, dux, rex superbus) in practically the whole Slavic territory. Particularly concrete information, however, we have from the areas of the Croatian, Slovene, Slavonian and Carantanian Slavs (the princes Vojnomír, Borna, Ljudevit and others), whose power rested on an army, strongholds (castellis, munitionum tantum castelli) and a princely retinue, and whose material culture of related character we find in the oldest inhumation cemeteries and strongholds.

The first prince of the Slavs living in the territory of present-day Slovakia and ancestors of the Slovaks to be attested in writing was Pribina (* c. 800 – † 861). From 825 to 833 he was prince of the independent Principality of Nitra, with its seat at Nitra (Nitrava).

After his flight from Nitra, to which he was forced by the military pressure of the Moravian prince Mojmír I, he spent several years seeking political support by turns from the margrave of the Frankish Avar and Carantanian marches and from the Bulgarian and Croatian (Slavonian) princes. In the end, from about 840, he received from the East Frankish ruler Louis the German, first in administration and later in lifelong tenure, the territory that we today call the Pannonian principality. Here he launched an extensive colonisation and Christianisation. His successor, and an ardent continuator of the Christianising activities, was his son Koceľ (* ? – † 876). He played an important role in supporting Christianity and in spreading it in the Slavic language through native priests, to which, at his request, the Byzantine missionaries Cyril and Methodius contributed.

The text of the Conversio chronicle gives a list of the names of the important people who took part in the consecration of the first church built by Pribina in Transdanubia. The list begins with 14 Slavic names, almost all of which, apart from three, are West Slavic: Chezil, Unzat, Chotemir, Liutemir, Zcurben, Siliz, Wlkina, Witemir, Trebiz, Brisnuz, Zuemir, Zeska, Crimisin, Goimer, Zistilo. Historians tend to regard them as members of Pribina’s retinue, that is, magnates loyal to him who fled from Nitra together with Pribina and in the new territory received new estates and became administrators of smaller settlement areas, of villages or even of larger administrative units of the principality of Blatnohrad. There follows a list of 15 purely German names, evidently of representatives of the Bavarian kindreds invited and resettled by Pribina, with a social status similar to that of the Slavic leaders mentioned above.

children.text: The main seat of Pribina and Koceľ and of their courts was Blatnohrad (Mosapurc, Civitas Priwinae, castrum Chezilons), today Zalavár, to the south-west of Lake Balaton. It consisted of three larger parts separated by fortifications: a fortified princely stronghold with a centrally placed governmental and ecclesiastical section, where a church and a monastery also stood, and a residential quarter, the bailey. Although for most of its existence it belonged territorially and administratively to East Francia, not only formally and structurally but also in the functional sense it was in fact more a Slavic than an East Frankish stronghold.

In the Middle Danube region, contemporary written reports at the beginning of the 9th century mention two kinds of Moravians, or Slavs in general, without the names of princes. The unification of the tribes here evidently took place as early as the 8th century, because at the assembly of the Frankish Empire in 822 their representatives were named simply as Moravians (Marahoni, Merehani, Moravi...). For their representatives we know no term that would have defined them precisely in legal terms. The terms used by the Frankish sources (primates, optimates, princeps, duces, regulus, rex, etc.) relate to the socially more progressive society of the Frankish Empire, or of the Eastern March and Pannonia, and are not directly attested for Great Moravia.

These magnates or tribal princes, knyazes (Old Church Slavonic kьnazъ, knjazi, knedz, Proto-Slavic kъnedzь <> from Old German kuning – prince, present-day könig, king), as representatives of the noble kindreds, “greater in origin and nobility” (maiores natu et dignitate), were elected by an assembly composed of the other noble members and representatives of the tribe, with the assistance, or even under the patronage, of pagan priests. The first strongholds were already becoming their seats, at first probably in the tenure and administration of the tribal community and its cult institutions.

After the expansion of the Moravian Mojmír I into the Principality of Nitra in 833, a polity arose that historians have called Great Moravia, and that contemporary sources call simply Moravia (Marahava, terra Maravorum, regnum Margorum, regnum Marahavorum). On its rulers, the Great Moravian Mojmírids, there exists a sufficient quantity of specialist literature, translations of early medieval written sources, popular-science works and belles-lettres and novels. This contribution therefore confines itself to very brief information on their historical deeds and life stories and offers rather a view, the main insights obtained by Slovak and Moravian settlement archaeology, especially of their seats of power. That is, above all the strongholds they had built, in which they resided, ruled and practised cult, and by means of which they organised society in terms of power and organised its defence against external enemies.

The Mojmírids were a kindred which originally ruled in the Principality of Moravia and later in the whole of Great Moravia, for roughly one century from the beginning (the first quarter) of the 9th century to the first decade of the 10th century. The fortunes of the kindred before Mojmír I and after 907 are not known, but one may consider that Mojmír I may already have had a blood-related predecessor from the time of the collapse of the Avar Khaganate, and also that some of its members from the collateral branches of the kindred ruled in Moravia until it was taken over by the Czech princes at the beginning of the 11th century. The kindred was named after its first known member, like the other ruling dynasties of the period (e.g. the Přemyslids, the Árpáds...), only by the historians of the 18th–19th centuries. Contemporary medieval writing neither knew nor used such a designation.

Mojmír I (* c. 800 – † 846?) became prince of Moravia from 830, and from 833, by annexing the Principality of Nitra, he became ruler of Great Moravia. From the available reports, or rather from the absence of reports, it is judged that he reigned and administered the principality in an altogether peaceful, non-expansionist manner. In 846 Louis the German deposed him, probably because he had after all finally attempted to free himself from tributary dependence on East Francia, and installed his nephew Rastislav in his place.

children.text: Under the rule of Rastislav, or Rastic (846 – † 870), the principality was stabilised and attacks by East Francia were several times successfully repelled. Although Frankish missionaries had been active in Moravia and Slovakia since the end of the 8th century, Rastislav and Svatopluk, in an effort to eliminate Frankish political influence, summoned the Byzantine scholars Constantine and Methodius to Great Moravia in 863 through the Byzantine emperor Michael III. Constantine created a script, the Glagolitic, for the needs of the Slavic language, so that Latin and Greek ecclesiastical texts translated into the native language could be put into book form. This act also laid the foundations of Slavic literature, and several secular texts were written in it as well.

Svatopluk (* 871 – † 894), who originally ruled in Nitra, became co-ruler of the principality after the “federalisation” of Great Moravia – to put it in today’s terminology – after 863. Following conflicts with his uncle Rastislav, he became the new ruler of Great Moravia, first with Frankish assistance and then after an anti-Frankish uprising. All these events were already recorded by the chroniclers of the period and evaluated by historians.

children.text: During his reign, extensive neighbouring territories in Central Europe were annexed to Great Moravia in several successful campaigns. There was massive construction and reconstruction of strongholds, the country reached the peak of its economic strength, craft production developed and the level of civilisation rose in general. After his death the annexed territories gradually broke away (Lusatia, Bohemia, Transdanubia, southern Poland), which, together with the disputes between his two sons – one was prince in present-day Moravia, the other in present-day Slovakia – weakened the country economically, militarily and ideologically. The attacks of the nomadic Ugrians, the ancestors of the Old Hungarians, then – after the conquest (Mikulčice, Strachotín, Pohansko, Bojná) or the capitulation of several important strongholds in Slovakia and Moravia, and finally the battles near Bratislava – destroyed the central political power of Great Moravia and thereby caused its collapse and fragmentation into many smaller units no longer capable of resisting the Old Hungarian tribes. These smaller polities, or rather their local leaders (the Poznans, the Hunts), mostly chose, step by step, various forms of submission, collaboration or even active participation in the further Old Hungarian conquests and in the later building of the Kingdom of Hungary.

children.text: According to the results of research by Moravian archaeologists, in the course of the 9th century a number of new strongholds arose as a manifestation of state formation in Moravian society under the leadership of the Mojmírid kindred, and at existing ones the old, simpler fortifications were replaced by structurally better-built ramparts, which is the case at Mikulčice and Nitra, or were replaced by fortifications in a different position, as at Olomouc, in the centre of today’s town, or at Uherské Hradiště – Staré Město, where the role of the main stronghold was taken over by the fortification in the locality known as Na Valech.

The numbers of Moravian strongholds given by the Bavarian Geographer for the two kinds of Moravians (Marharii, Merehanos) have to this day not been unambiguously interpreted. According to him, the Moravians (Marharii) had 11 and the other Moravians (Merehanos) 30 stronghold districts. Recently historians have inclined to the interpretation that the work should be speaking of 11 strongholds of the Moravian Slavs and 30 strongholds of the Nitran Slavs existing at the same time, some time after 833. In general it can be said that the number of these strongholds was not static: some disappeared for various reasons, others came into being. The greatest number of new strongholds arose or were structurally modernised in the times of Great Moravia’s greatest expansion and of its most powerful military activity, and of the beginnings of the Old Hungarian threat, under the rule of Svatopluk I.

children.text: The most important – and the only – Moravian and Slovak strongholds mentioned in the written sources of the 9th century, and that in connection with important military and political events, or with the presence of representatives of the ruling kindred and of the highest representatives of the church hierarchy, are antiqua urbs Rastici, or inefabilis Rastici Munitio, and Ch.r.dáb (or, in other translations from Arabic, Ghrád, Džerváb, Džarádist and the like), grad, Veligrad – that is, Rastislav’s old town and Rastislav’s impregnable fortress, and the great town and seat of the emperor Svatopluk. Further the town of Wábnít, “which is the first town in the east of the country”, then Nitrava, further Mosapurc, Mosaburg, Dowina, and Breslavaspurch.

Undoubtedly the most important fortified seats over the long term – in fact for the whole duration of the Great Moravian early state or principality – were the present-day archaeological sites at Mikulčice, Staré Město and Nitra.

The great lowland stronghold at Mikulčice, encircled by branches of the Morava, with an acropolis of 4.8 ha and with a fortified and unfortified bailey exceeding 50 ha, excelled not only in the size of its area and in the length, massiveness and quality of execution of its fortifications, but above all in the quantity and quality of its internal built-up area. (Fig. 8. The central stronghold of Mikulčice with its individual baileys, settlement areas and excavated sacral buildings)

Its roots go back to the 8th century and in the 9th century it is regarded as “Antiqua urbs Rastici, inefabilis Rastici Munitio” – the old seat of Rastislav and perhaps also of his predecessor Mojmír I. In the 9th century an unusual concentration of 12 sacral buildings arose here, along with a two-room stone palace building measuring 26 × 10 m, partly with a mortar floor and with an above-standard heating installation described as a fireplace. Within the fortified bailey a regular built-up area consisting of more than 200 dwellings, probably those of the military garrison, was also identified. In separate districts there were large workshops here, or also buildings which in technological terms may be described as of non-local ethnic origin, evidently also inhabited by foreigners – guests, asylum-seekers, higher members of princely retinues both of western, Bavarian or Frankish origin and from the eastern steppe milieu.

All this created a system that was, for its time, above standard, composed of the central princely court on the acropolis, of several satellite settlement units in the bailey, perhaps “manorial courts” also with sacral buildings and with advanced settlement contexts of ground-level dwellings, large and smaller production workshops, stores and granaries. The picture of this certainly dynamically developing, above-standard settlement complex is also reflected, approximately, in the quarter of a million artefacts from the almost 2,500 graves here. The above-average quantity and the craft and artistic quality of the gold and silver jewellery, weapons and other diverse artefacts of both local and foreign origin so far has no equivalent counterpart at the other Great Moravian strongholds, with the possible exception of Staré Město.

children.text: In the extensive agglomeration of Staré Město – Uherské Hradiště, exceeding 50 ha and considered to be the seat of Prince Svatopluk and of Archbishop Methodius (perhaps Ibn Yaqub’s Ghrád, Džerváb, Džarádist – the great town (grad) and seat of the emperor Svatopluk), there were several main functional, mostly fortified areas linked by routes – a power centre, an extensive central ecclesiastical area with a masonry church and further sacral buildings and a wooden monastery complex, several production areas, a central church cemetery, settlement satellites, and finally a separate island settlement with a dense built-up area and masonry architecture as well as a production component.

In the central power district at Staré Město, in the locality known as Na Dědině, by the church of St Michael, stood a building of palace type whose width reached 10 m and whose length was at least 18 m. It had all-stone walls laid in mortar and was provided with three kinds of poured mortar floors. The roof was formed of fired tiles of classical character, with decorative ridge tiles. It was built some time around the middle of the 9th century and soon afterwards a rectangular annexe with a mortar floor on stone packing was added to its northern side. This representative seat came to an end with the fall of Great Moravia. The remains of stone buildings that cannot be specified more closely are also known from Ostrov sv. Jiří (St George’s Island).

blocks.caption: Fig. 9. The settlement agglomeration of Uherské Hradiště – Staré Město with its individual settlement areas and sacral buildings.
blocks.alt: Fig. 9. The settlement agglomeration of Uherské Hradiště – Staré Město with its individual settlement areas and sacral buildings.

children.text: At Staré Město, in the locality known as U Víta, large post-built structures reaching an area of up to 100 m² were situated separately; these are mostly regarded as assembly places for the princely retainers or for other more important inhabitants or guests of the stronghold (merchants, craftsmen). In the area of the ecclesiastical precinct at Sady – a possible seat of Archbishop Methodius – a hall building about 32 m long stood in the second half of the 9th century, interpreted as a complex of dwellings of high church dignitaries, a monastic school and at the same time an assembly place for the inhabitants of the Christian precinct at Sady. There were also larger open spaces here, where inhabitants who left their villages in times of danger and took refuge behind the walls of the strongholds were temporarily accommodated. These may also have been places of markets or of popular assemblies and celebrations.

Nitra (Nitrava), as the seat of Prince Pribina with a church, mentioned for the year 828/830 in the Conversio, was after his expulsion in 833 the seat of Mojmír’s nephew Rastislav, and from 850 to 871 the seat of Rastislav’s nephew Svatopluk, as appanage princes of Nitra and, according to the principles then in force, heirs to the throne; and at the latest from 880 it was also the seat of the first bishopric in the territory of Slovakia, headed by Wiching. Archaeological excavations allow this stronghold and its sacral component to be located on the castle hill of Nitra, which was fortified from the first half of the 9th century and significantly rebuilt in the second half of the 9th century. Adjoining it, probably as a bailey, was an area reaching about 15 ha on the elevation Na vŕšku, above today’s Old Town. In the suburbium below the stronghold there were several village hamlets, the largest at Šindolka and Mikov dvor, as well as production workshops and cemeteries. There may also have been a solitary fortified area on Martinský vrch, with its own suburban hamlet.

The stronghold retained its tradition as the seat of appanage princes and heirs to the throne even after the fall of Great Moravia, when Nitra became, for a further century and a half, the seat of the appanage Principality of Nitra, headed by members of the Árpád dynasty and heirs to the Hungarian throne or their relatives.

children.text: The criteria of larger regional centres – which were certainly also the seats of more important magnate kindreds with their courts and retinues, and perhaps also places where part of the central military levy was stationed – were evidently best met by the Moravian strongholds at Břeclav-Pohansko, Znojmo-Hradiště, Brno-Líšeň, Olomouc – the stronghold in Moravia, Gars-Thunau in Austria, and by the strongholds at Bojná and perhaps also Bíňa, Zemplín, Majcichov and Pobedim in Slovakia. In all of these, or in the surrounding cemeteries, the presence of power-political, military and economic and mostly also sacral and cult components has been attested by the spectrum of finds, or can be assumed.

Several other larger strongholds may be considered as regional centres of middling importance, or as centres of smaller or less densely settled territories; these were perhaps the seats of lesser magnates who, at first independently and later by commission of the ruler, ensured the economic, administrative and military functioning of their settlement areas and guarded their main routes. They also supervised the collection and redistribution of payments in kind and taxes, the building and repair of fortifications, roads and bridges, the extraction of timber, stone and other raw materials, and the organisation of the defence of their stronghold.

A formally new category of fortified seat, with its own structure and specific functions, built more substantially in the Slavic milieu north of the Danube from the second half of the 9th century, were the magnates’ family manorial courts or small forts, which formally and functionally imitated the Frankish courts, whether curia regalis – royal courts – or curia nobilis – private seats of the nobility. In the earlier period these were above all the buildings of magnates inside additionally fortified strongholds, later mostly in open country as secondary seats of the nobility, manorial courts of rather economic significance. Their typical representatives are the manorial courts at Břeclav-Pohansko, Ducové and Zalaszabar in Hungary, by Lake Balaton. They were markedly smaller than strongholds, mostly had palisade fortifications, multi-room ground-level residential buildings that were above standard for the period, and churches – rotundas with a cemetery. In Moravia, manorial courts are further assumed at the strongholds of Brno-Líšeň, Strachotín and Nechvalín, but also within the stronghold areas at Mikulčice and Staré Město and at the Austrian stronghold of Gars-Thunau.

Today many of these abandoned early medieval strongholds are becoming the subject of interest not only of specialists, but also of local authorities and of numerous civic associations within their local-history, educational, heritage-protection and spatial-planning activities. With the help of joint projects, many Slavic strongholds are not only being further investigated but also reconstructed; they are becoming part of educational trails, being turned into museums, open-air museums and venues for regional events and international tourism, and they enjoy great interest from the wider public. Besides their own scholarly contribution to historiography, they are therefore also of benefit and inspiration to the educational, museum and environmental spheres. By combining in themselves elements of three activities – nature, culture and heritage – they are an attractive place for spending leisure time and for many cultural events; they are coming to life and thereby becoming once again an active, interesting and useful part of our environment.
A concluding note, as information for the wider interested readership and so that no superfluous polemical discussions should arise on the part of specialists:

Most of the borrowed illustrations used represent idealised, and in the older cases sometimes romantic or partly fanciful, conceptions of the individual authors and artists. For the most part these had no factual data at their disposal, either in the anthropological sense or in the field of clothing, its components, ornaments and armament, and in the case of equestrian pictures or statues, nor any insights into the riding equipment of early medieval social elites, that is, into a reality more than a thousand years distant. Or else they did not consult these details with specialists, which, however, is not their duty. Such a situation is quite common even among world-famous artists, and I think that within the scope of artistic licence they had the right to such work. After all, the illustrators and artists of the High Middle Ages likewise drew inspiration from the materials of their own time when depicting older figures, whether historical or legendary.
PhDr. Peter Šalkovský, DrSc., Institute of Archaeology of the Slovak Academy of Sciences in Nitra
